name: Iran

summary.text: Iran (the Islamic Republic of Iran since 1979) is a state whose relations with the United States and Britain run through a documented chain: the 1951 nationalization of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company and the 1953 coup against Mohammad Mosaddeq, planned and executed by the CIA and British intelligence; the 1954 oil consortium in which British Petroleum held 40%; the 1979 revolution and the seizure of the U.S. embassy on November 4, 1979; the 1985-86 U.S. arms sales to Iran examined by the Tower Commission and the Independent Counsel (Iran/Contra); the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action and the May 2018 U.S. withdrawal; the IAEA's 2025 reports and the Board of Governors' June 12, 2025 non-compliance resolution; and the June 21-22, 2025 U.S. strikes on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, followed by a public dispute between the administration's statements and a reported Defense Intelligence Agency initial assessment, and a Senate war-powers vote on June 27, 2025.

facts.claim: Under the 1954 consortium agreement that ended the crisis begun by the 1951 nationalization of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, Iran's oil operations were run by a consortium in which British Petroleum held 40%, Royal Dutch-Shell 14%, five U.S. majors (Standard Oil of New Jersey, Standard of California, Texaco, Mobil, Gulf) a combined 35% after transfers, Compagnie Francaise des Petroles 6% and eight independent American companies 5%. Encyclopaedia Iranica records the original memorandum as 40% AIOC, 14% Shell, 8% each for the five U.S. companies and 6% CFP.
facts.quote: The Consortium operates in Iran under an agreement reached in 1954 which terminated the crisis set off by Mossadeq's nationalization of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. in 1951. The members of the Consortium are British Petroleum (40%), Shell (14%), Standard of New Jersey (7%), Standard of California (7%), Texaco (7%), Mobil (7%), Gulf (7%), French Oil Co. (6%), and eight independent American companies (5%).

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1964-1968, Volume XXII, Iran, Document 179 (editorial footnote on the Consortium)
Oil Agreements in Iran

facts.claim: The 1954 consortium's operating rights ran for 25 years. A 1971 U.S. embassy telegram records the Shah telling the consortium that its rights would terminate after 1979; in 1973 the arrangement was replaced by a sale-and-purchase agreement under which the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) took over operations.
facts.quote: their rights will terminate after 1979

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, Volume E-4, Document 155: Telegram 7307 From the Embassy in Iran to the Department of State
Oil Agreements in Iran

facts.claim: After the 1979 revolution, the National Iranian Oil Company moved to end its joint-structure agreements with foreign oil companies. The Iran-United States Claims Tribunal, in Phillips Petroleum Co. Iran v. Iran, recorded that NIOC appointed a sub-commission of its board in August 1979 to end those agreements and negotiate new terms with former partners, and that notice to Phillips was given on 29 September 1979.
facts.quote: NIOC appointed in August 1979 a sub-commission of its Board of Directors to end the joint-structure agreements and negotiate new terms with former partners.

sources.title: Phillips Petroleum Co. Iran v. Iran et al., 21 IRAN-U.S. C.T.R., at 79 et seq.

facts.claim: On November 4, 1979, after the overthrow of the Shah and the return of Ayatollah Khomeini to Tehran in February 1979, Iranian students and militants seized the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and took 52 U.S. citizens hostage. The hostages were held for 444 days and released on January 20, 1981.
facts.quote: 52 U.S. citizens were taken hostage by Iranian students and militants at the U.S. Embassy in Tehran

facts.claim: The Tower Commission, the presidential review board that reported on February 26, 1987, found that the 1985-86 U.S. arms transfers to Iran became 'in fact a series of arms-for-hostages deals', that President Reagan 'did not seem to be aware of the way his arms-to-Iran policy was implemented', and that it found no evidence the President knew of the diversion of arms-sale profits to the Nicaraguan contras.
facts.quote: Almost from the beginning the initiative became in fact a series of arms-for-hostages deals.

sources.publisher: The American Presidency Project (UC Santa Barbara)
sources.title: Excerpts from the Tower Commission Report
The Tower Panel: Laying Out the Brutal Facts

facts.claim: The Final Report of the Independent Counsel for Iran/Contra Matters (Lawrence Walsh, 1993) concluded that the 1985-86 sales of U.S. arms to Iran contravened U.S. government policy and may have violated the Arms Export Control Act, and that the Iran and contra operations merged when money from the Iran arms sales was diverted to the contra effort in Nicaragua.
facts.quote: the sales of arms to Iran contravened United States Government policy and may have violated the Arms Export Control Act

sources.publisher: Independent Counsel for Iran/Contra Matters (via FAS)
sources.title: Final Report of the Independent Counsel for Iran/Contra Matters: Executive Summary

facts.claim: The Walsh report found that proceeds of the Iran arms sales were handled by the private 'Enterprise' of Richard Secord and Albert Hakim under Oliver North's direction; because funds were commingled, the Independent Counsel put the diversion to the contras that could have been proved at trial at $3.6 million and estimated the true figure at least $1.1 million higher. Fourteen persons were charged; four were convicted after jury trial, seven pleaded guilty, one case was dismissed, and on December 24, 1992 President Bush pardoned six defendants, including Caspar Weinberger, Clair George, Duane Clarridge, Alan Fiers, Elliott Abrams and Robert McFarlane.
facts.quote: Of the 14 persons charged criminally during the investigation, four were convicted of felony charges after trial by jury, seven pleaded guilty either to felonies or misdemeanors, and one had his case dismissed

sources.publisher: Independent Counsel for Iran/Contra Matters (via FAS)

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report on BCCI by Senators Kerry and Brown (December 1992) stated that BCCI was used by key Iran/Contra figures to finance arms shipments to Iran in connection with the Reagan administration's secret initiative, named Adnan Khashoggi and Manucher Ghorbanifar among BCCI customers involved in arming Iran, and recorded that documents on BCCI's financing of Iranian arms deals had been sealed in the United Kingdom by British intelligence and were unavailable to U.S. investigators.
facts.quote: BCCI was incontestably used by key Iran/Contra figures to finance arms shipments to Iran in connection with the secret Reagan Administration initiative.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (via FAS)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Chapter 11, BCCI, The CIA and Foreign Intelligence

facts.claim: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action of July 14, 2015 provided that for 15 years Iran would keep its enriched-uranium stockpile under 300 kg of UF6 enriched to no more than 3.67%, would redesign and rebuild the Arak heavy-water research reactor so that it would not produce weapons-grade plutonium, with the original calandria made inoperable by filling its openings with concrete, would build no additional heavy-water reactors for 15 years, and would provisionally apply the Additional Protocol to its safeguards agreement with the IAEA.
facts.quote: During the 15 year period, Iran will keep its uranium stockpile under 300 kg of up to 3.67% enriched UF6 or the equivalent in other chemical forms.

sources.title: Key Excerpts of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA)
Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, Annex I: Nuclear-related measures

facts.claim: The JCPOA took effect on 'Implementation Day', January 16, 2016, after IAEA Director General Yukiya Amano issued a report confirming that Iran had completed the necessary preparatory steps; Amano told the Board of Governors on January 19, 2016 that the way was clear for the Agency to begin verifying and monitoring Iran's nuclear-related commitments, and that Iran would provisionally apply the Additional Protocol from Implementation Day.
facts.quote: the way is now clear for the Agency to begin verifying and monitoring Iran's nuclear-related commitments under the JCPOA

sources.title: JCPOA Implementation Day Ushers in New Phase for IAEA in Iran: Director General Amano
IAEA and Iran: Chronology of Key Events

facts.claim: IAEA verification reports to the Board of Governors in 2018, before and after the U.S. withdrawal, stated that Iran had not enriched uranium above 3.67% U-235 and that its stockpile stayed within the JCPOA limit: the February 22, 2018 report (GOV/2018/7) and the August 2018 report (GOV/2018/33), which put the quantity of uranium enriched up to 3.67% at 139.4 kg as of August 18, 2018, against a cap of 300 kg of UF6 (202.8 kg of uranium).
facts.quote: Iran has continued the enrichment of UF 6 at FEP. Iran has not enriched uranium above 3.67% U-235, and as of 18 August 2018, the quantity of Iran's uranium enriched up to 3.67% U-235 was 139.4 kg.

sources.title: GOV/2018/33, Verification and monitoring in the Islamic Republic of Iran in light of United Nations Security Council resolution 2231 (2015)
GOV/2018/7, Verification and monitoring in the Islamic Republic of Iran in light of United Nations Security Council resolution 2231 (2015)

facts.claim: On May 8, 2018, President Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from the JCPOA and sign a presidential memorandum to begin reinstating U.S. nuclear sanctions on Iran. A White House fact sheet the same day described the decision as terminating U.S. participation in the JCPOA and re-imposing sanctions lifted under the deal; a Congressional Research Service report notes the decision did not invoke the Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act but rested on presidential authority to reimpose suspended sanctions.
facts.quote: Therefore, I am announcing today that the United States will withdraw from the Iran nuclear deal.

sources.title: Remarks by President Trump on the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action
President Donald J. Trump is Ending United States Participation in an Unacceptable Iran Deal
U.S. Decision to Cease Implementing the Iran Nuclear Agreement (R44942)

facts.claim: On July 1, 2019, the IAEA verified that Iran's stock of uranium enriched up to 3.67% was 205.0 kg, exceeding the JCPOA limit of 300 kg of UF6 (202.8 kg of uranium) for the first time since the agreement took effect.
facts.quote: the stockpile therefore has exceeded 300 kg of UF 6 enriched up to 3.67% U-235, which is 202.8 kg of uranium

sources.title: GOV/INF/2019/8, Verification and monitoring in the Islamic Republic of Iran

facts.claim: The IAEA's verification report of May 31, 2025 (GOV/2025/24) put Iran's stock of uranium enriched up to 60% U-235 in the form of UF6 at 408.6 kg (uranium mass) as of May 17, 2025, a net increase of 133.8 kg since the previous reporting period, produced at Fordow at an average of about 33.5 kg per month after Iran switched to 20% feedstock in December 2024. The Agency described Iran as the only non-nuclear-weapon state producing such material and called this of serious concern.
facts.quote: the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce such material

sources.title: GOV/2025/24, Verification and monitoring in the Islamic Republic of Iran in light of United Nations Security Council resolution 2231 (2015)

sources.publisher: Institute for Science and International Security
sources.title: Analysis of IAEA Iran Verification and Monitoring Report, May 2025

facts.claim: A separate IAEA report of May 31, 2025 (GOV/2025/25) gave a comprehensive assessment of undeclared nuclear material in Iran. It concluded that nuclear material and activities at three undeclared locations had not been declared, that the Agency could not determine whether that material had been consumed, mixed with declared material or remained outside safeguards, and that Iran had repeatedly either not answered or not provided technically credible answers to the Agency's questions and had sanitised locations.
facts.quote: Iran has repeatedly either not answered, or not provided technically credible answers to, the Agency's questions and has sanitised locations

sources.title: GOV/2025/25, NPT Safeguards Agreement with the Islamic Republic of Iran: comprehensive and updated assessment
IAEA Director General's Introductory Statement to the Board of Governors, 9 June 2025

facts.claim: On June 12, 2025 the IAEA Board of Governors adopted resolution GOV/2025/38, which found that Iran's repeated failures since 2019 to provide the Agency with full and timely cooperation regarding undeclared nuclear material and activities at multiple undeclared locations constituted non-compliance with its obligations under its Safeguards Agreement. It was the Board's first non-compliance finding on Iran since 2005.
facts.quote: constitutes non-compliance with its obligations under its Safeguards Agreement with the Agency

sources.title: GOV/2025/38, resolution adopted on 12 June 2025 (1769th session)
IAEA Board Adopts Resolution on Iran's Safeguards Obligations

facts.claim: The June 12, 2025 Board resolution passed by 19 votes in favour, 3 against (Russia, China and Burkina Faso) and 11 abstentions, according to Russia's envoy to the IAEA and contemporaneous reporting; Israel struck Iranian nuclear sites the following day, and Iran responded to the resolution by announcing a new enrichment site.
facts.quote: the resolution was adopted in the IAEA Board of Governors by 19 votes in favour

sources.title: IAEA Board of Governors passes anti-Iranian resolution — Russian envoy
UN nuclear watchdog says Iran in breach of obligations, Tehran announces counter-measures
Iran threatens nuclear escalation after UN watchdog board finds it in breach of obligations

facts.claim: The Office of the Director of National Intelligence's 2025 Annual Threat Assessment (March 2025) stated that the intelligence community continued to assess that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and that the Supreme Leader had not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003, while noting Iran had undertaken activities that better positioned it to produce one if it chose. DNI Tulsi Gabbard repeated this in her opening statements to the Senate and House intelligence committees on March 25-26, 2025.
facts.quote: continues to assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and Supreme Leader Khamenei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program that he suspended in 2003

sources.publisher: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
sources.title: Annual Threat Assessment of the U.S. Intelligence Community, 2025

sources.publisher: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
sources.title: DNI Gabbard Opening Statement as Delivered to the HPSCI on the 2025 Annual Threat Assessment
Trump, Gabbard Comments on Iran Nuclear Capability

facts.claim: On June 20, 2025, asked about Gabbard's March testimony, President Trump said she was wrong and that Iran was very close to a nuclear weapon. Gabbard then posted on X that the intelligence community's position was that Iran could produce a nuclear weapon within weeks to months if it decided to finalize the assembly, and that her testimony had been taken out of context; a CBS News report said a U.S. intelligence summary found Iran could build a device in months but had not assessed that Iran had decided to do so.
facts.quote: But the summary did not assess that Iran had made a decision to sprint toward a nuclear weapon.

sources.title: One U.S. report assessed Iran was 3 to 8 months from nuclear weapon — but no sign it planned to, intel sources say
Trump says US intelligence 'wrong' about Iran not building nuclear bomb
Tulsi Gabbard Reacts After Trump Said She Was 'Wrong' About Iran's Nuclear Threat

facts.claim: On the evening of June 21, 2025 (early June 22 in Iran), U.S. forces struck the Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan nuclear sites. In an address from the White House that night, President Trump said the strikes were a spectacular military success and that Iran's key nuclear enrichment facilities had been completely and totally obliterated, and that the objective was the destruction of Iran's nuclear enrichment capacity.
facts.quote: Iran's key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.

sources.title: Transcript: President Donald Trump addresses nation after US strikes on Iran
June 21, 2025: Address to the American People
U.S. strikes 3 nuclear sites in Iran, in major regional conflict escalation

facts.claim: At a Pentagon press conference on June 22, 2025, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine described 'Operation Midnight Hammer': a strike by U.S. Central Command on three Iranian nuclear facilities involving more than 125 aircraft, including B-2 bombers, fighters, tankers and a guided-missile submarine, with decoy flights and more than two dozen Tomahawk missiles fired at Isfahan. Caine said initial battle damage assessments indicated all three sites sustained extremely severe damage and destruction but that final assessment would take time; 14 GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrators were reported used at Fordow and Natanz.
facts.quote: Initial battle damage assessments indicate that all three sites sustained extremely severe damage and destruction

sources.title: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine Hold a Press Conference
Pentagon reveals how B-2 bombers struck Iran nuclear sites in mission dubbed 'Operation Midnight Hammer'
Joint Chiefs chairman supplies new details about MOP bomb attack on Iranian nuclear sites

facts.claim: In a statement to the UN Security Council on June 22, 2025, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said craters were visible at Fordow, Iran's main site for enriching uranium to 60%, indicating the use of ground-penetrating munitions by the United States; that no one, including the IAEA, was in a position to assess the underground damage at Fordow; that additional buildings at Isfahan and the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant had been hit; and that Iran had informed the IAEA there was no increase in off-site radiation levels at the three sites.
facts.quote: no one - including the IAEA - is in a position to assess the underground damage at Fordow

sources.title: IAEA Director General Grossi's Statement to UNSC on Situation in Iran, 22 June 2025
Update on Developments in Iran (5)

facts.claim: On June 24, 2025, CNN reported that an early Defense Intelligence Agency assessment, based on U.S. Central Command's battle damage assessment, found the strikes had not destroyed the core components of Iran's nuclear program and had likely set it back only by months; other outlets reported the assessment found centrifuges largely intact and that the DIA labelled it low confidence with analysis ongoing. The White House press secretary said the reporting was inaccurate, and Secretary Hegseth said the campaign had obliterated Iran's ability to create nuclear weapons.
facts.quote: The Defense Intelligence Agency produced the assessment, which was based on a battle damage assessment by US Central Command after the strikes.

sources.title: Exclusive: Early US intel assessment suggests strikes on Iran did not destroy nuclear sites, sources say
Strikes on Iran set back nuclear program by several months, sources say
New U.S. intelligence report suggests Iran's nuclear program only set back by months after strikes

facts.claim: On June 25, 2025, CIA Director John Ratcliffe issued a statement that a body of credible intelligence indicated Iran's nuclear program had been severely damaged by the strikes, citing new intelligence from a historically reliable source that several key facilities were destroyed and would have to be rebuilt over the course of years; CNN noted it was unclear whether this was an official agency assessment or the Director's view, and that the statement did not specify whether the damage was from U.S. or Israeli strikes.
facts.quote: CIA can confirm that a body of credible intelligence indicates Iran's Nuclear Program has been severely damaged by the recent, targeted strikes.

sources.title: Statement from Director John Ratcliffe about Intelligence on Iran's Nuclear Program
CIA says it has evidence Iran's nuclear program was 'severely damaged' as assessments of US strikes' impact continue

facts.claim: On June 27, 2025, the Senate rejected, 47-53 (Record Vote 328), Senator Tim Kaine's motion to discharge S.J.Res.59, a war-powers resolution directing the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities against Iran not authorized by Congress. Senator Rand Paul was the only Republican to vote yes and Senator John Fetterman the only Democrat to vote no.
facts.quote: Motion to discharge the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations rejected by Yea-Nay Vote. 47 - 53. Record Vote Number: 328.

sources.title: S.J.Res.59 - 119th Congress (2025-2026): A joint resolution to direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran that have not been authorized by Congress
Friday, June 27, 2025
Senate rejects attempt to rein in Trump's power to wage war on Iran

facts.claim: After the strikes, IAEA Director General Grossi said the Agency did not have information on the whereabouts of Iran's stock of highly enriched uranium, which the IAEA estimated at 440.9 kg enriched up to 60% as of the June 2025 conflict. In March and April 2026 he said the widespread assumption was that much of the material remained in the Isfahan tunnel complex, but that the IAEA had not been able to inspect it or confirm that its seals remained in place.
facts.quote: We are the IAEA, so we are not speculating here. We do not have information of the whereabouts of this material.

sources.title: IAEA director says Iran's enriched uranium can't be located following US military strikes
UN nuclear chief: Much of Iran's highly enriched uranium likely still buried at Isfahan site
Much of Iran's near-bomb-grade uranium likely to be in Isfahan, IAEA's Grossi says

facts.claim: The October 1973 oil embargo was imposed by the Arab members of OPEC against the United States in retaliation for the U.S. decision to resupply the Israeli military, and extended to other countries that supported Israel; it banned petroleum exports to the targeted countries and introduced production cuts. Iran, which is not an Arab state, is not listed among the embargoing countries in the State Department's account or in the CIA's October 19, 1973 memorandum, which named Libya, Abu Dhabi, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia as having announced or threatened a total embargo.
facts.quote: several countries, including Libya, Abu Dhabi, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia, have either announced or threatened a total embargo against the United States

facts.claim: At the conclusion of the OPEC meeting in Tehran on December 23, 1973, Iranian Finance Minister Jamshid Amouzegar announced a new posted price of $11.60 for Persian Gulf crude, an increase of more than 100 percent, according to a State Department telegram to the embassy in Tehran. The same telegram cites a December 21 Tehran cable summarising a conversation in which the Shah told Ambassador Helms he was considering pushing OPEC for a new crude pricing arrangement at the Tehran meeting.
facts.quote: at the conclusion of the OPEC meeting in Tehran on December 23, Amouzegar announced a new posted price of $11.60 for Persian Gulf crude, an increase of more than 100 percent

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXVII, Iran; Iraq 1973-1976, Document 49: Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Iran

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXVII, Iran; Iraq 1973-1976, Document 48

facts.claim: In a December 26, 1973 telegram, Ambassador Helms reported on the Shah's December 23 press conference, noting that the new prices would hold only for the ninety days after January 1, 1974 and that the Shah wanted to use that window to set crude prices against the cost of other energy sources.
facts.quote: these new prices will hold only for the ninety days after January 1, 1974

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXXVI, Document 271: Telegram From the Embassy in Iran to the Department of State, December 26, 1973

facts.claim: A CIA report of January 4, 1974 described the December 1973 Tehran price decision as a compromise between the $5.50 per barrel increase favoured by the Shah and the $1.25 per barrel rise reportedly suggested by Saudi Oil Minister Yamani. A December 1973 telegram from the embassy in Saudi Arabia reported Saudi officials saying they had been against the increases and that the Shah was chiefly to blame.
facts.quote: a compromise between the $5.50 per barrel hike favored by the Shah and the $1.25 per barrel rise reportedly suggested by Saudi Oil Minister Yamani

sources.title: International Oil Developments, January 4, 1974

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXXVI, Document 276: Telegram From the Embassy in Saudi Arabia to the Department of State

facts.claim: Iranian Foreign Minister Zahedi told U.S. officials in December 1973 that the price disruption had originally been caused by American companies submitting bids of $16-18 per barrel for Nigerian oil; French Foreign Minister Jobert likewise warned the Secretary of State that the $22-23 per barrel auction prices paid by American independent oil companies would be used as a pretext to justify higher OPEC prices.
facts.quote: Zahedi thought, however, that the mistake had originally been made by American companies submitting bids for Nigerian oil of $16-18 per barrel.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXVII, Iran; Iraq 1973-1976, Document 48

facts.claim: In a 1974 memorandum recommending a personal letter from President Nixon to the Shah, Secretary of State Kissinger wrote that the Shah's interest in maintaining high oil prices ran counter to the U.S. interest in seeing them lowered.
facts.quote: the Shah's interest in maintaining high oil prices runs counter to our interest in seeing them lowered

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXVII, Iran; Iraq 1973-1976, Document 57: Memorandum From Secretary of State Kissinger to President Nixon

facts.claim: In August 1974 Treasury Secretary Simon said he wanted a confrontation with the Shah over oil prices and thought the Saudis would reduce prices if the Shah went along. On August 27, 1974 the U.S. embassy in Jidda reported that Saudi Oil Minister Yamani said the Saudi Cabinet had agreed to hold the line against any price increase at the September OPEC meeting, where Iran was demanding a 35 percent rise.
facts.quote: The Cabinet had agreed that at the OPEC meeting the end of September Saudi Arabia must hold the line against any price increase.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXXVII, Energy Crisis 1974-1980, Document 79: Telegram From the Embassy in Saudi Arabia to the Department of State

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXXVII, Energy Crisis 1974-1980, Document 1: Memorandum of Conversation

facts.claim: In November 1974, after more than four hours with the Shah in Tehran, Kissinger reported by backchannel to Scowcroft that the Shah would recommend a slight cut in oil prices at the next OPEC meeting, to be maintained through 1975, which Kissinger estimated at a 20 to 25 percent real reduction over two years; the Shah made the cut conditional on absolute secrecy. A follow-up message said the Shah would propose a single price system, about $1.65 below the existing $11.65 level, and a freeze of crude prices for the first nine months of 1975 at the December 12 OPEC meeting.
facts.quote: the cut is conditional on our maintaining absolute secrecy

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXVII, Iran; Iraq 1973-1976, Document 87: Backchannel Message From Secretary of State Kissinger to Scowcroft (Tehran)

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXVII, Iran; Iraq 1973-1976, Document 89: Backchannel Message From Secretary of State Kissinger (Tehran)

facts.claim: In September 1975 President Ford wrote to the Shah ahead of the OPEC price decision, arguing that another increase would hurt the U.S., European, Japanese and developing economies. In his reply the Shah listed reasons why he believed an oil price increase would be justified and argued that consumer taxes could absorb any increase.
facts.quote: In his response, the Shah listed reasons why he believed an oil price increase would be justified, and argued that consumer taxes could absorb any increase.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXXVII, Energy Crisis 1974-1980, Document 80: Telegram to the Embassy in Iran (letter from President Ford to the Shah)

openQuestions: The owner characterizes the June 2025 strikes as 'unwarranted'. The record shows: the DNI's March 2025 assessment that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and that the Supreme Leader had not authorized the program suspended in 2003; the IAEA's May 31, 2025 reports (408.6 kg of 60% HEU, unresolved undeclared-material questions) and the Board's June 12 non-compliance finding; the administration's June 20-25 statements (Trump: 'she's wrong', 'completely and totally obliterated'; Ratcliffe: 'severely damaged'); and the reported DIA initial assessment that the program was set back by months. No primary document reviewed here states that Iran had decided to build a weapon, and none settles the degree of damage; whether the strikes were 'warranted' is a judgment the sources do not make.

The 1979 oil step is sourced only to the Iran-US Claims Tribunal award on NIOC ending joint-structure agreements (Aug-Sept 1979) and to a 1971 cable on the consortium's expiry after 1979. A petroleum-museum page says the consortium agreement was 'cancelled in March 1979' but this is single-sourced; a NIOC or FRUS 1977-80 source for the formal termination was not found.
The official whitehouse.gov transcript of the June 21, 2025 address was not surfaced by search; the quote is from the ABC News transcript and the Miller Center archive, which agree on the wording.

The official DoD transcript page is now hosted at war.gov (the renamed defense.gov); the search returned only excerpts, so the aircraft count (125) and the 14-MOP figure rest on the transcript excerpt and CBS/DefenseScoop reporting respectively. The owner should confirm against the full transcript.

The Walsh report quote on 14 persons charged (four convicted, seven pleas, one dismissal) was returned from Part XI/Summary of Prosecutions excerpts; the pardons list is in the Summary of Prosecutions. Two of the 14 (Weinberger and Clarridge) were pardoned before trial, which the per-person outcomes in summpros.htm detail.
The June 12, 2025 Board vote tally (19-3-11) comes from the Russian envoy's post as reported by TASS and from France 24/Tehran Times; the IAEA's own press release with the tally was not surfaced.

The IAEA 2016-2018 compliance facts rest on GOV/2018/7 and GOV/2018/33 excerpts; the February 2018 stockpile figure was not captured. GOV/INF/2019/8 is the first report showing the 300 kg limit exceeded.

The Senate BCCI report's Iran-arms material is in Chapter 11; the report also records the CIA's testimony (Acting Director Kerr) that the agency had no involvement in BCCI's use for arms to Iran, and that the extent of U.S. official involvement in some BCCI-linked Iran arms sales could not be determined. The NBC allegation that William Casey met Abedi is recorded by the report as an allegation, not a finding.

The Shah's December 1973 Iranian oil auction price was not found in a primary document. An EBSCO summary gives a Japanese high bid of $17.80 per barrel for NIOC's surplus-oil tender, and FRUS vol. XXVII Doc. 48 records Zahedi citing $16-18 bids for Nigerian oil and Jobert citing $22-23 auction prices; the FRUS telegram on the Iranian auction itself was not surfaced and the figure should not be used until it is.

FRUS vol. XXVII Doc. 49 gives the December 23, 1973 posted price as $11.60; Doc. 89 (November 1974) refers to 'the existing $11.65 level'. The owner should check which figure applies to Arabian Light versus the Persian Gulf marker.
The 1973-75 items above are drawn from FRUS vol. XXVII (Iran; Iraq) and vol. XXXVII (Energy Crisis 1974-1980) as well as vol. XXXVI; the Iran-specific price documents sit mostly in vol. XXVII.
